HEEWON STYLE — a KOREAN WEBTOON movie still PAINTED like a premium digital painting, the look of a dramatic manhwa cover. A 2:1 movie frame composed for a 2:1 letterbox crop (nothing important at the top or bottom edge). The shot the scene names (wide establishing, two-shot, close-up, over-the-shoulder) from a dramatic camera angle (low three-quarter, worm's-eye, high overhead or dutch), never a flat straight-on catalogue pose. Named characters' FACES are drawn exactly like the attached character sheet: the same confident ink linework drawn BOLD and THICK with real line weight — a heavy tapered black contour around the whole silhouette and the hair mass, medium lines for folds and features, fine lines only for lashes and loose strands and manhwa face design (eye shape, brows, nose, jaw, hairline and hair), recognisably those characters, in the clothes the scene gives them. EVERYTHING ELSE IS PAINTED: visible textured brushwork — loose digital-paint strokes and dry-brush, charcoal-like hatching that follow every fold of the silk and every plate of armour, the shadows built from layered strokes, the brightest ridges laid in with single confident strokes, a faint paper-and-canvas grain; at the edges of the garments the linework breaks into loose sketchy strokes. MYTHIC PAINTED FINISH: rich saturated jewel-tone colour, never a muddy grey-brown wash; splashed sumi-ink spatter and dry-brush flying-white streaks breaking out at the frame edges; ONE bold sweeping painted ribbon of the scene's accent colour (cloth, smoke, banner, mist or light) carving across the composition like a brushstroke of legend. NOT flat cel-shading, NOT smooth airbrushed gradients, NOT a clean vector look, NOT photoreal, NOT 3D. Low over the river water at dawn, a Tang tower-ship's prow towering into frame from the left. ONE device: a line of tower-ships receding up the river in a long diagonal into mist, completely PLAIN deep red sails, no emblem. On the prow platform, three metres above the water, the old marshal Su Dingfang points upriver; beside him Xue Rengui in a white war coat over steel lamellar holds his halberd upright. Oars dip in unison along the hull; spray, mist, a pale low sun behind the fleet. Quiet before the landing, not a battle. REFERENCE SHEET. TOP ROW, left to right: LEFT face = sudingfang, SECOND face = xuerengui. Copy each face exactly; give each person the dress the scene names. SMALLER SECOND ROW, left to right: ship_tang (copy its exact shape). RED FOWL Colour #d95f4b. XUE RENGUI Colour #e8e3d5. SHIPS: copy the attached ship board for each kingdom exactly (hull shape, mast count, sail colour and battens) and keep that same ship in every still of the scene. Boards are design only: ignore their bright daylight sky and calm sea, repaint the ship in the scene light. 7th-century timber ships only, never European hulls, cannon or funnels. TRUE SCALE (real 7th-century measures; a man is 1.65 m): ships are drawn life-size against their crews and against each other, never toy boats with giant men. A man standing on deck is about 1/15 the length of a 24 m warship and 1/20 of a 35 m tower-ship; a deck bulwark reaches his chest; the waterline is two men's height below a warship deck. Dozens of men fit along one side of a warship, each one small against the hull, masts four or five men tall. When two kingdoms' ships share a frame, keep their real length ratio. Tang louchuan tower-ship: huge dark timber hull with a multi-storey deck castle, two or three masts of deep red battened sails, the largest ship on any sea. Size: the flagship tower-ship is about 35 m long and 8–9 m wide, deck about 3 m above the water, its three-storey castle rising about 12 m (seven men tall), up to two hundred men aboard; the ordinary Tang warship is about 24 m long with forty to ninety men, its deck a man's height higher than any Yamato or Baekje boat. Its broadside looks like a city wall. BACKGROUND AND LIGHT (painterly tenebrism): the background IS the place and the moment of the scene — open sky if they are in the sky, the hall if they are in a hall, the gate, the river, the snow — painted loosely in atmospheric brushwork (drifting smoke, cloud, haze, mist, falling snow, embers) in the scene's own colours, soft and out of focus, with a faint bokeh of small lights; it has colour, weather and depth — never a flat black void, never a detailed set; crowds and armies only as massed painted shapes dissolving into haze. ONE hard directional key light that belongs to the place (a brazier, a lamp, the sun through cloud, a torch, moonlight) rakes across the faces and clothes from the side or from below, modelling them in high contrast with deep painted shadows and a thin edge of the same light along the silhouette. Each character's colour lives in that light and in the atmosphere around them — never a glow aura or halo. Faces and bodies act the beat: real expressions, real weight, mid-motion. Faces from the sheet; new poses, never the sheet's stance. Each named person appears once, never cloned. Everyone wears period clothing of their own court (Korean, Tang, Yamato, Mohe furs), never European dress. No text, no speech bubbles, no panel borders, no watermark. DAY GROUND: the frame is built on WHITE — a high-key, paper-white ground: pale bright sky, white haze and mist, sunlit plaster and pale stone dissolving into bare white paper at the edges, the shadows few, crisp and cool-grey; the figure is the dark, inked thing in a bright frame. Never a black void, never a dim dusk wash.
